items.attribution: Adapted from the Unit 8 period review
items.exemplar: (a) The embargo exposed how dependent the postwar consumer economy — built around cars, suburban homes, and cheap gasoline — was on imported oil, producing shortages and a new sense of vulnerability. (b) Stagflation combined rising inflation with rising unemployment at the same time, breaking the Keynesian toolkit that policymakers had relied on to manage the economy. (c) The second energy crisis, together with the televised Iranian hostage crisis, fed a sense of national decline that helped a growing conservative movement argue the postwar bargain had failed — opening the way for Reagan's election in 1980.

parts.prompt: Identify one way the OPEC oil embargo of 1973 affected the American economy.
Explain how stagflation challenged the economic assumptions of the postwar decades.
Explain how the energy crises of the 1970s contributed to the political developments of 1980.

items.stimulus_text: In 1973 the OPEC oil embargo exposed American vulnerability to imported energy, and a second energy crisis followed in 1979. Stagflation — inflation plus unemployment at once — broke the Keynesian toolkit that had guided postwar economic policy. In 1979 Jimmy Carter told the nation it faced a "crisis of confidence."

items.attribution: Adapted from the Unit 7 period review
items.exemplar: (a) Wilson's Fourteen Points called for a League of Nations, along with open diplomacy and national self-determination. (b) In the 1920s Congress passed immigration quotas aimed at southern and eastern Europeans and Asians, reflecting the same inward turn that had killed the League fight. (c) The Senate's rejection of the League shows isolationism — the impulse to avoid foreign entanglements — contending with internationalism, a tension that also shaped the 1898 debate over whether a republic should hold colonies and the later failure of the Neutrality Acts to keep America out of war.

parts.prompt: Identify one provision of Wilson's Fourteen Points.
Identify one development of the 1920s that reflected the country's inward turn after the League of Nations fight.
Explain how the debate over the League of Nations illustrates a recurring tension in American foreign policy.

items.stimulus_text: After World War I, President Wilson proposed a League of Nations as part of his Fourteen Points plan for peace. The Senate rejected American membership in the League, and the country turned inward.

items.attribution: Adapted from the Unit 4 period review
items.exemplar: (a) The Embargo Act of 1807 and then the War of 1812 cut Americans off from British manufactured goods, forcing them to make their own — so domestic factories grew. (b) The Erie Canal linked the Great Lakes to New York City, tying distant regions into one commercial web and making New York the commercial capital. (c) Shared pride after the War of 1812, combined with regionally linked markets and the wider circulation of goods and ideas, helped Americans imagine themselves as one nation rather than a collection of separate regions.

parts.prompt: Identify one way the War of 1812 or the Embargo Act of 1807 contributed to the growth of American manufacturing.
Explain how the Erie Canal or other transportation improvements changed the relationship among American regions.
Explain how the Market Revolution contributed to the development of a shared American national identity in the early 1800s.

items.stimulus_text: The War of 1812 ended in stalemate, but it produced a wave of national pride and new factories. Canals like the Erie (completed 1825), steamboats, turnpikes, and railroads then tied distant regions into one commercial web in what Americans called the Market Revolution.
